title: The monk at Bosra
hookLine: the sirah tells of a Christian monk, Bahira, who saw signs in the boy on a caravan to Syria

lines: A MONK'S CELL BY THE ROAD.
HE NEVER SPOKE TO THEM BEFORE.
cards: A stone cell by the trade road near Bosra, on the edge of Syria. Caravans from Mecca have passed it often, and the monk inside has never spoken to them, the sirah says. This time he does.
He sends word to the travelers: I've prepared food, and I want every one of you to come, young and old, slave and free. The merchants of Quraysh look at each other. What's changed?

teach.b: The caravan belongs to Abu Talib, and he has brought his nephew, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, still a boy. Ibn Ishaq tells the story.
The monk is named Bahira, a Christian who, the sirah says, had learned from a book kept in that cell.
From his window he has seen something: a cloud shading one traveler as the caravan came in, and a tree bending its branches over him where he sat. At the meal, the boy isn't there.
He's been left with the baggage, the youngest.
Bahira insists: bring him. Then he watches him closely, and asks him questions.

teach.h: HE WON'T SWEAR BY THE IDOLS.
teach.b: When Bahira asks in the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the idols of Mecca, the boy refuses to be asked by them. Bahira asks in God's name instead, and the boy answers.
Finally the monk looks at his back and sees a mark between his shoulders.
Bahira turns to Abu Talib with a warning: take your brother's son home, and guard him carefully. And Abu Talib does. How should this be heard?
Al-Tirmidhi records a version of the journey too, and some hadith scholars have questioned parts of it, so it's honest to hold the details lightly. What stays is the shape.
On a dusty road, a stranger from another faith looked closely at an orphan boy left with the bags and saw something worth protecting.
The sirah keeps this Christian monk in the story with respect, as a neighbor who recognized goodness when it walked in.

how: The story of Bahira is told in sirah books and classes about the Prophet's ﷺ youth, with some teachers noting which parts are well supported and which are weaker.

o: a Christian monk who saw signs in the boy
a merchant who ran the caravan to Syria
a Meccan poet who praised the young boy

games.q: the monk at Bosra — tap the pairs.
p: take him home and guard him

s: the boy was at the meal from the start
he'd been left with the baggage; Bahira insisted they bring him.
the boy refused to be asked by al-Lat and al-'Uzza
Bahira asked in God's name instead, and he answered.
every detail of the story is beyond question
some hadith scholars have questioned parts of it.

games.q: you're Abu Talib. a monk you've never met tells you your nephew is special and must be guarded. what do you do?
o: laugh it off and go on to Syria with him.
take him home and guard him.
games.why: the sirah says Abu Talib took him back, as Bahira urged.

practice: Think back to someone who saw something good in you before you saw it yourself, a teacher, a coach, an older cousin, a stranger even, and let their face and their words come back.

Then turn it around: is there someone near you, left with the bags, so to speak, whose goodness no one has named yet? If you pray, you can ask Allah to open your eyes to it; if not, just hold that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Bahira. A Christian monk on the road to Syria, who, the sirah says, saw signs in the boy and told Abu Talib to guard him. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: someone saw it early. Tomorrow, the league of the virtuous. Until then.
